utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties had some preliminary matters to raise. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just very briefly, last week, during cross-examination, at transcript page 26926, I mentioned that I would not follow up further with the witness regarding the relationship between the positions of Chief of Staff and deputy commander under the brigade rules but would seek agreement with the Defence. Mr. Lukic and I discussed it this morning. My understanding is that the parties are in agreement that under the JNA brigade rules, the Chief of Staff is also the deputy commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see you're nodding yes so apparently there was agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it is hereby put on the record that the parties agree that under the JNA brigade rules, the Chief of Staff is also the deputy commander of the brigade. We consider this an agreed fact. That was your preliminary matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was ours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. And the Defence has to explain the position with the experts as Your Honours asked from us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I'm also a bit confused with the developments in this area. I just learned over the weekend that nothing is disclosed in regard of our expert reports. And I got the report from my staff that expert report done by military expert is finalised in B/C/S. It's sent for translation, but I was explained that it has to be arranged, all the documents have to be uploaded, and because of the influx of Defence witnesses, our support staff is not capable of dealing with -- with the -- this material and we will have to find a way how to, I don't know, probably ask the Registrar to help us with the -- new members of our team since it's obvious that with the manpower we have right now we will not be able to finish this work. I don't -- I heard that it won't be a -- possible before the end of the case. So because it's really a lot of work. But I can tell you that -- so military expert finished his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I do not understand is, is a matter of uploading or selecting or -- what is it that causes such problems that it cannot be done within the next year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every expert report has documents that support that expert report and those documents have to be found in the system since to check whether there are already parts of the admitted -- admitted documents, admitted evidence, or not, or it's a new document, and all those documents have some strange numbers so it's not possible just to compare the number and have the problem solved. So -- but I'll promise that I will work with my staff to solve the problem and hopefully we'll have some help from the Registrar on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in general term, I would say that to the extent possible, the Registrar always tries to assist at the best of its abilities any party in resolving problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I -- if I may continue, because I am pretty lost myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On 2nd of October we received translation of supporting material of military expert. On the 25th of September, we received a translation of aerial bombs expert report on aerial bombs. We are expecting translation on Sarajevo shooting incidents on the 24th of October. On the same date we should receive translation of Markale 1 and II expert reports and on shelling incidents of Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's four translations in one day to be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shootings incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Markale II is one -- one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Markale I and II. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's one. On 17th of November this year, we should receive translation on demographic expert report, and we received B/C/S reports on Saturday from mining experts. It's mining of religious and sacral buildings. And we received expert report in B/C/S from the communication expert, also, I think, on Saturday. But the biggest problem are those ... Markale I, Markale II, mining expert, and shooting -- shooting incidents from Sarajevo because they have the most documents and they have very strange numbers with the -- the pictures or documents that follow that expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But where do these numbers come from? I mean, strange numbers. Someone must have invented the number, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I only know that staff has a great problem, great deal of problems with those numbers. Some -- many of them are downloaded from the Tribunal site but the numbers do not match anything that we use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Numbers from other cases? Or have you tried to understand where and --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's very long numbers. It is not ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not exhibit number. It's not ID doc number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then the expert could explain where the numbers come from, isn't it? The experts are responsible for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They did, but still it's not possible to track in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what is their explanation? What are these numbers in their view?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They say that they downloaded from the Tribunal site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question I would have put to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can inquire again. We did inquire. We did seek the explanation from them. But obviously it's -- somehow it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, if it would be possible to match them with an existing documentary system within the Registrar, then I'm quite confidence that the Registry could give some help. Let's try to get the right answers to the relevant questions. I think that's the first step, very important to be taken. Apart from that, if translations of the expert reports are there, then I would suggest that at least the reports themselves are already disclosed even if not the full supporting material is there yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only that those supporting materials inside the reports would have those strange numbers, so I don't know how much would it be workable for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least I take that apart from the numbers that at least the Office of the Prosecutor would be able to orient itself on the gist of what the experts are telling.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Any disclosure of reports in whatever format would be of assistance at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They might even have a clue for your strange numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps they turn out to be lucky numbers then. That's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll give the instruction to my staff members to disclose whatever we have in our possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as soon as the translations are ready, and I do understand that in four days from now a new series of three will be there to disclose them without delay to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes, not because it is a CLSS fault, but sometimes these translations are late because we dumped a lot of documents on them already, the witness statements and so on. So it doesn't mean that we are going to receive these on these dates but we hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's scheduled for the 24th, I understand. And the aerial bombs on the 25th of September, that report is available in translation by now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you mentioned the date of the 25th of September but I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it should be translated already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you have not disclosed that yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, because of those numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that whatever -- however odd the numbers may be that at least what is there, available in text, that that is already disclosed and I do understand that it's there already for a month and the Prosecution has not yet had the benefit of looking at it. Anything further on the matter, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we will close whatever we have in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile I address the -- one matter that is the associated exhibits and the MFI relation to witness Vladimir Lukic. During the testimony of Vladimir Lukic, a number of documents were MFI'd. The parties were instructed to review and identify those portions they wished to have in evidence. At the end of the testimony, the Defence was also invited to provide a revised list of associated exhibits that it was tendering with this witness. The Chamber hereby -- the Chamber would like to receive an update on this matter and perhaps not now immediately, but if any progress has been made, the Chamber would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The ball is in my field, Your Honours. Mr. Traldi did his part of the work. I just have to finalise the table --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This week for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I am afraid that football is played with one ball but I'm afraid that there's a lot of balls on your half of the pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I realise that, Your Honour. I'm working hard to solve all the troubles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just as a final matter while the witness is being brought in, Mr. President. There was one issue with the transcript on Thursday that I discussed with my learned friend and I wasn't sure how he intended to handle it. It related to one of the questions on direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was agreed that I probably should ask to re-open the direct since there is one word entered on the page 26897, rows 24 and 25, when I asked the witness about Tomislav Batinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was entered that he was killed. Maybe I misspoke, but the position is that that gentleman is still alive. He was wounded. So whatever Your Honours think is the best to clarify that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can say we wouldn't have any objection to briefly reopening re-direct -- or sorry, briefly reopening direct to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, good morning. First of all, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was one matter remaining from last Thursday. You were asked about Mr. Tomo Batinic; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said that something happened in November 1992 with him; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the question suggested that he was killed, but parties agree that he was wounded and you have confirmed this now. So, therefore, I think, Mr. Lukic, that the matter is sufficiently resolved. If you -- would you like to add anything or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that on that day, he was inspecting one of the lines facing Pale municipality with the security officer from the brigade command. On their return, they drove over an antitank mine, that, on that occasion, the driver got killed whereas Mr. Batinic sustained severe injuries. He lost one eye. He was wounded to his leg. He had pieces of shrapnel in his head, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do understand well that he is still alive today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, he is still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Traldi, please proceed. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination, Mr. Ujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P166.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, this morning, I want to start with the operations conducted by the Rogatica Brigade in late May 1992. This is a document dated the 23rd of May bearing the name Rajko Kuzic. This is being sent through Sokolac, and if you look in the top right corner, you can see the identification for military post 1132, that was the post number for the 2nd Romanija brigade based in Sokolac; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in the addressee line, we read Supreme Command of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and commander of TO Sokolac. Do you know who Mr. Kuzic would have meant by Supreme Command of the Serb Republic of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a rule, the supreme commander of the armed forces of any army or any country is at the same time the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in this document, Mr. Kuzic refers to armed operations conducted on the 22nd of May "enemy strongholds in the villages of Dub, Prokrivenik, Kopljevici, Kozici, and Cadovi and also against Pasic Kula, Rajs Laze, and Rudo 2." At the end of the document, he writes that the Rogatica Territorial Defence unit will conducted an attack on Oskoplje. Now the villages I have just mentioned, those were all Muslim villages; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, only you made one mistake. Rather than on the 22nd of May, as it's written here, it should read the 2nd of May, not 22nd. I see that it's written 22nd. Yes, these are all Muslim villages from which attacks came at the minority Serb community. Probably he decided to prevent these attacks and to try to attack with counter-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You said these were -- you said this should read the 2nd of May, that the Rogatica Territorial Defence attacked -- the Serb Territorial Defence attacked these villages. Were you recorded correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You said it was on the -- on the 2nd of May. I'm just drawing your attention that it's not the 2nd of May but 22nd of May which is consistent with the document which says 22nd day. Maybe it was a mistranslation that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Either way I'm happy to see we agree it's the 22nd that is at issue.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31450.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that Mr. Traldi, I'm a confused about military post 1132. You said Sokolac. That was confirmed by the witness. The stamp reads Ljubljana. Is there any explanation either to be given by the witness or do the parties agree on why it says Ljubljana which is not the same as Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't have a submission to make in that respect at the moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I sought confirmation of the post number in other documents but hadn't sought an explanation for Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the stamp you looked at a second ago said military post 1132. You confirmed that it was Sokolac. At the same time, I see Ljubljana appearing in that same stamp. Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I know, and whether that's sufficient or not it's up to you judge, I suppose that this military post used to be located in Ljubljana. Later on, after it moved from Slovenia it went to Sokolac. Probably they still had the same old stamp which says Ljubljana and that is why it appears on this document. This is as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The stamp not being updated. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, what we're seeing on the screen now, is a regular operations report from the Serbian Army of BiH Rogatica Brigade command to the RSK command dated 31 May 1992. And if I could direct your attention to point 6 this will require us to turn to page 2 in the English. We see a note on the expenditure of fuel and ammunition. 1500, 7.62 millimetre bullets; 160, 82 millimetre shells; 120, 60 millimetre shells; five, 120-millimetre shells and others. Now this related to ammunition expended by the Rogatica Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it reads. However, I claim that in each report the commander always pictured larger expenditure of ammunition so as to be able to request more from the brigade in order to have a reserve at his disposal. That is why these figures are so high: 1500 bullets, 2.000 bullets, 160 shells, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The types of ammunition reflected in the report, those are all types of ammunition that were used by the Rogatica Brigade in operations in late May; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I see for 120-millimetre shells he's only listed five pieces. So he hasn't overstated that one significantly, has he?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because there was only one 120-millimetre mortar at the time. We only used such shells in absolute necessity. If we had to target a very precise military target when we were certain we wouldn't miss. Plus, it was costly ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask that this document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31450 receives number P6828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're seeking it to be marked for --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm in the Chamber 's hands as how best to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you want to do with it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We would certainly -- we certainly will seek to have it admit at some point during the Defence case but we can use it again with another witness regarding the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not tender it now right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm happy to tender it now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm -- if it is about the discussion we had last week with Mr. Ivetic about knowledge of the witness of events, et cetera, it again directly relates to what you asked the witness. The witness has given some evidence about it. And as I said last week, when I ever used in this context the word bar table it would be wrong. It is documentary evidence directly linked to evidence the witness has given. In this case, he has told us his knowledge about the way in which such numbers are presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll tender the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not object to this document. Only I would have one intervention regarding the transcript and it's in regard of this document. So we do not object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, you have given the -- let me see.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number is 6828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, you wanted to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, on page 13, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says "absolute necessity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the witness said and I quote [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask him to repeat what he said, which is always -- -

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can check audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no, no. You said there was only one 120-millimetre mortars at the time and you used such shells only under what circumstances? Could you repeat what you said that you used such shells only in ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had one mortar and we seldom fired from it. Only in crucial moments when a target was bigger in size and needed to be dealt with, then we used the 120-millimetre pieces. I do repeat we used it seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you want me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we have first now given the witness an opportunity to repeat what he said but apparently you have a different recollection, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He said [B/C/S spoken] and it's really a military term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We now heard you speaking B/C/S in English. Could we -- could you slowly repeat what you just said so that we receive translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Decisive defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you use the words "decisive defence" in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we were under attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's your -- you have used those words that's the only thing I wanted to verify. Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, turning to another set of operations - and I am done with this document now - you mention in paragraph 32 of your statement, now Exhibit D691, attacks on the villages of Kozadre, and Kramer Selo and you say that: "The Serbs asked them to surrender their weapons or else the villages from which weapons were fired would become military targets. This is what happened." Now, those villages were both majority Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Kozadre was just to the west of Gucevo where your company was based; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you co-ordinated the artillery on the attack on those villages; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. We only used 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your view at the time was if there's fire coming from a village it's not a village anymore. It's a military target; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a legitimate military target, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 26 of your statement, you say that after operations in Rogatica began, Serbs moved with their families to the suburbs and Muslims moved out in the direction of Sarajevo, Gorazde, and some Muslim areas of Rogatica. Now, in these villages, Muslims, in fact, fled from the shells your brigade fired and were in such a hurry to escape that they left behind wounded children, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, the Muslims started leaving Rogatica right after the police force was split up before the war. Serbs left too because both felt insecure. Serbs went to those parts of the city where Serbs were in the majority or to their native villages. The Muslims, I assure you went to Sarajevo before the war broke out. There was a large group which left lawfully before that. Another group went for Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about the Muslims in these village, Kozadre and Kramer Selo. They fled from these attacks in a column and in such a hurry that they left behind wounded children, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what you're trying to ask but that's not the case. In Kozadre there were no refugee Muslims from Rogatica and other villages. Only domicile Muslims, local Muslims. When --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly slow down and repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slow down and repeat your answer. If would you please resume from, "In Kozadre there were no refugee Muslims from Rogatica and other villages. Only ...," and could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the inhabitants of Kozadre village. In Borovsko some of the population was from Rakitnica which is neighbouring village, and when those columns of refugees from Rakitnica were withdrawing, they left behind three wounded children. On my orders, the soldiers brought them in to the out-patient clinic. They were taken to Rogatica as well where their wounds were treated. Then they were sent to the Sokolac military hospital in Podromanija. They were treated there, and handed back to their families once they were fully recovered. I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now your information was those children were wounded by shrapnel during the attack; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But no one targeted children. We were trying to target their fighters who were occupying a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So to go back to my original question. This column of refugees you've described, they were fleeing this attack and they were fleeing in such a hurry that they left behind wounded children, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. They didn't flee. They were simply withdrawing under fire. They were using infantry weapons. They were accompanied by the column of people as well as the armed personnel who were withdrawing under fire. They returned fire as well. The artillery was using mortars and we couldn't see the column. That is why the children became wounded by shrapnel but spread. But, as I said, we treated them, recovered them, and handed them back to their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, your brigade also incorporated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask some --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few more questions about this. First of all, you said they didn't flee. If there is mortar fire to your village, and women and children are leaving, would you not call that fleeing? Is there any -- because the common understanding of the word "fleeing" is trying to get away from a place which is not safe for you. Therefore, I have some difficulties in understanding the way in which you describe what happened and, at the same time, saying that they were not fleeing. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The unit of the Muslim army which opened fire from the village, when responded to by our side, they retreated. They withdrew. And with them, as I see now, went the civilians. So it wasn't fleeing per se. But it was a combat procedure. I'm retreat, returning fire, in order to get out of a certain territory. That is the meaning of what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We -- we understand that that's your understanding of what "fleeing" means also for women and children. Then you said the armed personnel were withdrawing under fire. And you said: "The artillery was using mortars and we couldn't see the column." You were talking about your artillery, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you fired those artillery assets without being able to see the column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. We used a particular sector from which we opened fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you couldn't see what you -- you had no -- no people in front observing where the mortars landed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were aware that women and children were still accompanying, as you said, the military personnel that were withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I know. I didn't know it at the time. We were simply opening fire and there was a legitimate military target. I was plotting co-ordinates based on the fire we were receiving from that sector. I tried to match those co-ordinates with our artillery fire. I didn't see who was in the column, and I learned only later what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness said -- you can check page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 20. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe he could remove his headphones. He does not speak any English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't speak English, Mr. Ujic? You do not speak English or understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could you take us -- off your earphones for a second. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In line 19, I heard that the witness said: We were simply opening fire at, not that we were simply opening fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's why he said there was a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can clarify, Your Honour, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understood this as being firing at where the witness knew was a military target, which, a legitimate military target which implicitly says that what we were firing at. That's my understanding of the language. And I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He wanted to say that the fire was opening in their direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, let me then see. Okay. That's at least not what was translated. Let me see. I did understand -- but again I'm checking with the parties and with my colleagues. I did understand that he considered the firing from the opposite side to create a situation where there was a legitimate military target to fire at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how we understood, Your Honour, and that's what is -- what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So everyone understands that. So apart from whether this is legally sound or not is a different matter as everyone will certainly understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Right. Just to clarify, and perhaps I'm confused, it says in the subsequent sentence on the transcript, "I was plotting co-ordinates based on the fire we were receiving from that sector," and I'm just inquiring whether Mr. Lukic is suggesting anything different. I'd understood that to be the witness's explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If is it clear, then we do not want to propose anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- I'll nevertheless try to -- yes. Can I ask you a few questions about your plotting the co-ordinates. You said you were plotting the co-ordinates based on the fire you were receiving from that sector. Was that co-ordinates on a road? Was that co-ordinates on a specific position and fire is to be understood how? Was that mortar fire? Was that small-arms fire? Was that rifle fire? Could you tell us a little bit more in detail what you observed and how you plotted those co-ordinates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy to. As the commander of the unit, I had a topographic map with me, a pair of binoculars and since I am an artillery man by military speciality I could use the map to plot the co-ordinates based on what I observed with my binoculars. I used the three co-ordinates in order to provide sufficient firing elements to the artillery, and I could issue a command to target that particular location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you couldn't see the column. What you did then see with your binoculars that allowed you to -- to plot those co-ordinates on your military map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the binoculars, I could see where the fire was coming from. They even used 62-millimetre mortars to launch shells in our direction and then I used binoculars to locate their positions of firing. I then used that as our target for the counter-attack. However, we truly could not see any column moving there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have some difficulties in understanding how a withdrawing column with women and children would use mortars on their move-out and what you meant by a counter-attack. Could you -- I mean, I see a column, I do understand the column moving out, withdrawing, together with women and children. Would they use mortars, stop for a while, install the mortar, and then fire those mortars, and then take them up again and then move further? Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a 60-millimetre mortar is a small one. It's an anti-infantry weapon. And a soldier can carry it and can fire it basically moving. All it needs is to be placed on the ground, fired and then it can be moved again. It doesn't have a stand that needs to be dug in. It's an infantry weapon that one carries on one's back as a rifle almost. And that's how shells can be fired. That is what I could see through my binoculars. Wherever they tried to fire those, we targeted that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you could see them firing through your binoculars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was a plume of smoke and the place where the flash would occur. That marked the place where the shell was fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you see the flash, then you must have a view more or less on the people who are manning that, because the flash doesn't go up very high in the air. It's just at the mouth of the tube, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. However, only two men are in the crew, and the column that was withdrawing was not close to the firing position. It was perhaps in a valley or in a depression withdrawing. Those who fired, however, were visible to me. I could see them through my binoculars firing at our positions. So, to repeat, no one intended to target the column. That was the least or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The last thing we wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if people in the column are hit by the shrapnel, they must have been pretty close to your target, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably if they were hit by shrapnel they must have been close. But I suppose, I do not claim I suppose, that they were on a lower ground and then a piece of shrapnel wounded the children, so they must have been within 50 to 100 [Realtime transcript read in error "1.000"] metres of the landing the shell. That's how the children became wounded by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you saw those using mortars and you didn't see the people in a column 50 or 100 metres away from that because ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I claim responsibly that the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a few questions also. Sir, this column that was withdrawing, you say it was withdrawing not fleeing, do you know where it finally ended? Where they went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose they went in the direction of Vragolovi village, where a large group of refugee assembled, and from there on to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the last sentence the witness said. Could he please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... suppose. You don't know for a fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I suppose because they could retreat there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said a little earlier that you picked up these children who were wounded, got them dressed up, and when they recovered you handed them over to their people. You remember saying so? Where did you hand them over if you didn't know where the people went to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that I ordered that the children be taken away because they were in inaccessible terrain. The Serb soldiers brought them in their arms to the ambulance where they were -- when they were taken to Rogatica. They were administered first aid and then sent to the hospital in Sokolac. They were treated there, and in Sokolac they were handed back to their families who by that time had been in Sarajevo. We allowed for the families to come to pick up the children. In any case, the children were fully treated. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long were they treated for, these children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wouldn't know precisely. They suffered minor injuries in their legs. There were more like scratches or through wounds, so, in any case, small-intensity wounds. Perhaps they were treated for a fortnight, up to a month, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you mentioned that this column went in some direction. Now you're saying that they were handed over to the parent in Sarajevo. I'm not quite sure where you say these children were handed over. Who were their parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I recall, it was the Pasic family from the village of Rakitnica. They had two children and there was a grandmother.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The mother said that the father was in Sarajevo. Could the witness kindly repeat the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat the rest. You're speaking a little too fast for interpreters. Can you slow down and repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, the two children and their mother were wounded. I repeat, lightly wounded. When they were recovered, the mother said that her husband was in Sarajevo and that they were going to go to Sarajevo. According to the information I had, they were placed in a vehicle, transported safely close to Sarajevo, where the husband took them over. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the children when they were taken for treatment, they were taken together with their mother, who was also injured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a clarification for the record. You told us about how the children were wounded by shrapnel and you said they have must have been within 50 to 100 metres of the landing of the shell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was recorded 50 to 1.000 metres and this is now a correction for the record. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifty to 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was a bit confused by two of your answers. Earlier you said that the children were taken to Rogatica, then they were sent to the hospital in Sokolac, and then you said they were treated and in Sokolac they were handed back to their families who, by that time, had been in Sarajevo. But I now understand that the mother, at least, was part of the family as well, I would say, was with the children already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. And she said that she wished to go to Sarajevo for them all where her husband was, and under escort, they were taken from Sokolac and then handed over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the column still withdrawing when you found these children? Or was combat over by then? That's not a good question, I think. Was the column still withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the 2nd of August, 1992, in the evening hours. It was summer time, could have been at around 2100 hours or 2130. When I heard that there were children wounded, I told them to carry them out. And, after that I didn't get any further information as to where the column went and which route it took. It was the early -- end of a combat day that was almost over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Almost or completely? Was there any further combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Traldi, these were a lot of questions after you asked about children left behind. It's time for a break. The Chamber is not stealing any from you. As you know, it is always carefully recorded how much time we take and, therefore, there's still quite some time left for you. Witness, we would like to see you back this 20 minutes. We take a break. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I have a few questions to follow up regarding the attack we just discussed. First: What type of mortars was your brigade using during that attack?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 62-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Rakitnica today, and in your statement you mention Kozadre -- sorry, Kozadre and Kramer Selo. Was Rakitnica also part of that attack?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A small intervention. I think that page 28, line 11, should be clarified. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll re-ask the question if that suits my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so and see whether any objections then remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to re-ask, during this attack, what type of mortars did your brigade use?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, during the attack, our brigade used solely 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Rakitnica today, and in your statement you mentioned Kozadre and Kramer Selo. Rakitnica village was also attacked as part of the same attack; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Rakitnica was dealt with by the Sokolac TO I believe one day before we dealt with Kozadre. As for Kramer Selo, which is right opposite the road on the road to Sarajevo, this was dealt with by Socice TO. Therefore, I did not take the route, the road with my unit to Kramer Selo but instead --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the road that he mentioned last.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the road you mentioned last, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, viewing at the road Sarajevo-Rogatica, Kozadre village is on the right-hand side of the road. Opposite, on the left-hand side of the road, is Kramer village which was dealt with by Socice TO, whereas Rakitnica was dealt with by Sokolac TO because it is closer to Sokolac. The unit and I only had the task to do Kozadre and ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't understand the last name that the witness pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you said the unit and you only had the task to do Kozadre and one other place. Can you very slowly repeat the name of that other place?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borovsko, village of Borovsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Borovsko and Rakitnica, those were both also Muslim villages; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Rakitnica and Borovsko were mixed villages. Albeit the majority was Muslim but there were Serb families as well in both villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned the Sokolac TO. These operations, I believe you said, were conducted in August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I believe that it was the 1st of August when the TO Sokolac did Rakitnica because territorial-wise, it wedges into the territory of Sokolac municipality and that is why they dealt with these villages instead of us. We never touched Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So my specific question was by August 1992, the Sokolac TO, like the Rogatica Serb TO, had been transformed and was under the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, when the attack began, it was directed at the villages, not at a column; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack was directed at enemies firing groups with the aim to unblocking the Rogatica-Sarajevo road, since these two villages, Kramer Selo and Rakitnica suffered check-points where there were casualties. There were even people killed. Kozadre, on the right-hand side of the road, and Rakitnica, on the left-hand side, erected barriers and check-points on the road where we suffered losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, this material is also in your statement. Let me try and ask the question in a different way. The column fled after the attack; right? The attack was initially directed at the villages from which you say the fire was coming; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can never agree with that because that was never our aim, that is to say, to target civilian columns, but exclusively enemy firing groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the moment about your aim; I'm asking at the moment: The column fled after the attack; right? The attack was not initially directed at the column.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you put it, it seems that that is right. But there was no fire opened at the column. This was not a standard, classic column. It was just a withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not listening carefully to the question. What Mr. Traldi wants to know is whether the column only started after you had fired at the village. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can give you the following answer: A village wasn't shelled. It was not attacked. Only the location of the outgoing fire. If it was in the village, then the village became the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the column only started after you had fired at targets in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We launched an infantry attack. If there was fire coming from the village, or mortar fire, that became a legitimate target which we neutralised. We fired at it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, apparently you either do understand my question or you don't want to understand my question and were more focussed on telling us what you consider important. You may proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn to a different topic now. Your brigade also incorporated some volunteers from Serbia who said they were Arkan's Men, Jovic's Men, and Seselj's Men; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they conducted some of the urban warfare during your operations; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And they wanted to conduct urban warfare because they thought there was more wealth in town because their motive was looting; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can say that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can 65 ter 31328 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This, sir, is an commendation to your brigade and the 2nd Romanija Brigade, dated the 26th of December, 1992, and apparently signed by General Galic. We read here: "The great and immeasurable contribution of your fighters and units is embedded in the Army of Republika Srpska's magnificent successes in 1992." This reflects the SRK's approval of your brigade's activities in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was a greeting document, let's say, for the new year and for Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Specifically, it was a greeting that reflected their approval of your activities in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Military ones. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31328 receives number P6829, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can we have 65 ter 31331.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, sir, you state in paragraph 35 of your statement that: "The Muslim villages of Satorovici, Okruglo, Tmorni Do, and Osovo which did not want conflicts and had surrendered their weapons enjoyed full protection." So I'm directing your attention now to the fourth paragraph of this document, at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S. It refers to a man named Sejdalija Mirvic, and the article reads: "His village of Satorovici near Rogatica was entirely emptied of its remaining Muslims today. The Serbian authorities came to each" - and here I think we need to turn to the next page in the B/C/S - "to each Muslim household and told the families to prepare to leave. Then they were bundled on buses to Sarajevo." Now, that's the truth, isn't it, that the Muslims of Satorovici were sent to Sarajevo in 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it reads. In that period, I was the chief of defence in Rogatica. I was involved in things relating to defence with the army, and I cannot tell you anything more about this because I didn't know anything about it at the time. If they left, I believe that was true, since somebody wrote about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, this is published in the "New York Times" several thousand miles away from Rogatica. I put it to you that it's not credible that the readers of the "New York Times" in 1994 were aware that the Muslims of Satorovici were sent to Sarajevo and that you've never heard of it before today. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I heard it today for the first time. I had heard but I don't know how many of them left and who organised the transportation. I was involved in completely different tasks. And it didn't concern me at the time in that aspect. I know what had happened before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When did you hear that they'd been sent to Sarajevo in 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, officially -- officially -- is there a problem? Officially, I never received any document to that effect that -- somebody would inform me in writing. I just heard it in conversations orally. And that would be towards the end of that year, but only sketchy details. I cannot tell you a lot about it because I was not privy to this. Therefore, I cannot contribute anything. But what happened, happened. I am not refuting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: According to this paragraph 35 in your statement, you say that these people enjoyed full protection. Who gave them the protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these villages had been loyal to the authorities of Republika Srpska. As I said earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Who provided them protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the civilian authorities, as well as military structures. They provided protection from both their extremists and Serbian extremists as well. So we had both the civilian and the military component participating in the protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Civilian and military components of which ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, power was exclusively in the hands of the Serbs, and they protected this village as they did any other village, irrespective of whether they were Muslim or Serbs. They just had to be loyal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. But now if the military and civilian authorities of the Serb people provided them with protection, and you don't dispute what is written in this document, what happened that they got emptied of this and taken to Sarajevo when you were protecting them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is beyond any doubt that the fact is that we protected them. However, what happened then, as I sit here today, I cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you're not answering my question. My question is: These people were under the Serbian military and civilian protection. What happened that they got bundled into buses to Sarajevo when they were under your protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was a member of the brigade, they were under protection. Upon my departure and taking up a new post, I wasn't in the brigade any longer, and the civilian authorities, the president of the municipality, and the chairman of executive committee took care of these people. Therefore, I cannot tell you what happened. I can see that something happened, but what triggered that and why, I really cannot answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- while you were head of the brigade, you provided them with protection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. Not only in terms of security and safety, but also the provision of food. I personally took medicine to General Asim Hodzic, who lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31331 receives number P6830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn now to some questions about persons detained in Rogatica municipality. First, Mehmed Agic. You visited him when he was detained; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, he was an important prisoner; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of the joint TO before the war. After the division of power, he continued to be the commander of the Muslim TO, and, as such, he was a captive. He was a neighbour of mine in the apartment complex, and as soon as I learned that he was in detention, I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I think you've answered a different question. I hadn't at the moment asked about your relationship with Mr. Agic. All I'd asked was: He was an important prisoner; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you perhaps say that again a little bit more slowly for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: Absolutely. Mehmed Agic, by virtue of his office, was a very important prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As such, his capture was reported to your brigade's superior command, the SRK corps command; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't me who informed the command but, rather, I received information over the radio that he had been captured. Probably the commander used his own channels in order to pass on this information, that this person is in our custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd refer the Chamber to Exhibit P4387.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Agic was captured along with several other people and brought to the Sladara malt house by Mr. Ljubinac; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that since at the time he was driving an APC, he used that vehicle to the area of imprisonment and he took him to the Slad factory. I know that I saw him there a couple of times while he was in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31352.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And while it comes up, did Rajko Kusic also go to the Sladara factory to see Mr. Agic?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that since I was closer to the Slad factory, I was the first to arrive there and I saw Meho Agic there. Some 15 minutes later, Rajko Kusic came as well because he had received this information. So for a while we were together with Meho, and then Rajko Kusic stayed behind while I left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is Mr. Agic's statement which he swore was truthful under oath. If we could turn to the bottom of page 5 in English and 11 in the B/C/S, and I think if we could -- the one on the right is now correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of the page, he mentions that you and Mr. Kusic visited, and we see that discussed in the bottom few lines. Turning to the next page in both languages, just a few lines from the top, he describes a conversation and then it says: "Soon afterwards Kusic, Ilic, and two or three of their henchmen went to the room opposite us and started beating Milic and two members of the Hodzic family who had been captured with him." Now, to be fair, I'll say that he indicates he was blindfolded at the time. So my question is: Is he correct that you were still there when those persons were beaten?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim with full responsible before this Court, in view of my solemn declaration, that I went to see Mr. Agic as a neighbour and a friend. While he was lying with blindfold, I said, Good morning, neighbour. Would you like a cigarette? And he said, Gladly, Mile, and he lit a cigarette. Now, what is written here is something that I'm not familiar with that, because when the commander came, I left the room, and I don't know if something happened or not. While I was there, he wasn't touched at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't say he was touched. He says people in the opposite room were beaten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat: While I was there, nobody, really nobody, was beaten or beaten up. On the contrary, there were talks but I remained for a short period of time. After I had left, I don't know. I cannot tell you what happened, if anything. I didn't hear anything and I don't know if anything happened at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Unless the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Unless the Chamber has additional questions, I would turn now to the Vlahovic school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question but I'm rather addressing you. You said, in all fairness, that person was blindfolded. Where do I read that he was blindfolded when he was transported to a different location? I do not read that at that point in time when he was visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But when I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My understanding was it had been on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That may --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's my recollection, Mr. President, towards the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you wait for a second -- please move on and I'll have a look at the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, sir, turning now to Vlahovic school. You suggest in your statement and in your testimony last week that people went to the school voluntarily. I have several questions about this. First, on at least one occasion, you yourself saw armed soldiers escorting people to the school; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did state that. It concerned the part of town called Gracanica. They had to be taken through the part of town that had not been liberated where there were armed Muslims. They were some placed under escort by soldiers for their protection. It was a smaller group of perhaps some 15 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were aware that your subordinate, Mr. Ljubinac, has been conflicted of crimes against humanity in Bosnia for, among other things, participating in the forcible transfer of women, children and adult men to the Vlahovic school; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was proven in one of the judgements by the BiH court and I will not comment upon it. Court decisions are not something to be commented upon but obeyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now can we have Exhibit P6803. As it comes up, this will be a regular report from the Rogatica Brigade to the SRK command dated the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the first paragraph, your brigade reports: "There was no significant enemy activity in the brigade's zone of responsibility. Large numbers of Muslims, mostly women and children, are arriving in the town every day. The people are being moved into the premises of the secondary school centre." Now, I have a couple of questions for you about this language and I note it is signed for Mr. Kusic. First, you testified last week that people of various ethnicities were held in the Vlahovic school - Muslims, Serbs, Croats. Mr. Kusic is only mentioning Muslims, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he says. However, I claim before this Court because I went to the school once and I saw what I saw, that there were Serbs, Croats and people from mixed marriages, entire families that were accommodated there. They were there so as not to lose their lives in the conflict with the other side. That was the basic reason why it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If there was no significant enemy activity in the brigade's area of responsibility, why would they have feared losing their lives?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply put, at the beginning of the war, people on both sides who were in town felt insecure because one could never know whether there would be a knock on the door and someone would be killed. So people sought refuge in safe places, safe shelters. The Veljko Vlahovic school was one such place in Rogatica at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You have referred to the Vlahovic school again now as a safe place and a safe shelter, as you did last week. In fact, you know crimes, including sex crimes, were committed against the people there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately -- well, I was actually talking about the period at the beginning when it was envisaged as a collection centre. At the time it was truly a safe place for all those who felt insecure to stay in their own homes. Now, as for what happened later, it seems things did happen as I could see in judgements and statements, and that that is the extent of what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At the moment I'm not asking about judgements and statements. I'm inquiring about your evidence in paragraph 29 of your statement, D691, that you heard that police who guarded the Vlahovic school had raped women who were detained there, that you demanded that the perpetrators be punished, and that you were told, "that this was a war, that people's lives mean nothing, and that I should not meddle in their business." So for the moment I have only one focussed question for you about this: Approximately when did you first receive this information? What month and what year?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, it was in 1992. It could have been, I think, late July or early August. But most likely in late July. I went to the school personally to visit the people who were up there. I distributed some cigarettes, spoke to them. And then one of the ladies who was present there confided in me because she had known me before the war, and she told me some things. When I was leaving the secondary school building, I came upon the police station commander. I directed his attention to it and he said that I shouldn't meddle in their affairs, and that it was police business, whereas I was with the army. He also said that human lives are worth less than vegetables these days and that I shouldn't get involved for fear of being liquidated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly repeat the very end of his answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said after "for fear of being liquidated."

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For fear of being liquidated. It was said that human lives were worth nothing, and I was afraid to be killed myself. That is why I never went back to the school and I did not get involved in any things that had to do with the police. They had their own command system. They received different orders. And from that moment on, I withdrew. I no longer went to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What was the name of the police station commander who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen Vasiljevic was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you didn't mention this incident in your Karadzic evidence, your evidence in the Karadzic case here, and you testified in the Paunovic case in Bosnia that you were told not to come back to the Vlahovic school because you were -- you had given a detainee cigarettes. When did you recall that you were told not to meddle in the rapes that had been committed there?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, I don't think I was asked in the Karadzic case, but I believe it was contained in the statement in that case, unless there was an oversight. So sometime in late July, I was told those words. I claim it was the case. And perhaps it slipped through the cracks in that previous statement, but it did resurface again before the BiH court and now, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn now to Rasadnik and if the Prosecution could please have 65 ter 26044.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it comes up, approximately how far was Rasadnik from the Sladara building, which was the Crisis Staff headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the Crisis Staff. The brigade command was never at Sladar. As we can see on the map, if we go to the very left side of the screen, we see the Rasadnik facility. To the right and below is the malt factory or Sladar. So maybe it's 3 to 400 metres, the distance between the two facilities, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going ask the usher to assist, please, and I'm going to ask you to make three markings on this image and to wait, please, for my instructions before making each of the three markings. So, first, I'd ask that you circle the Sladara building.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And next to it, write a "KS" for Krizni Stab.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sorry, before you mark again, what's the building to the left of the circle that you've just drawn? Immediately to the left.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a silo of the commodity's reserve agency which is still in operation today. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The silo was what I was referring to, yes. Please don't mark that. I'll ask you now to circle the area of Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And perhaps it would assist if I --

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. There's no need. I worked there for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And make an "R," mark an "R."

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at the bottom, if you could mark your initials and today's date, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In the white area at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 20th, if the parties would agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it's the 20th of October, 2014.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very good with dates. So October the 20th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to move away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And just your initials -- oh, you've marked your initials, I see, next to the R.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we can agree that that is sufficient, I'd tender the image 65 ter 26044 as marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The third marking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If it is clear, we can erase the initials. I'm in the Chamber's hands, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not the practice in this Chamber that always markings have to be made -- have to be accompanied by initials and a date, because by their admission and by being stored in the e-court, that's enough. But I do understand that the witness gave his initials just below the "R" for "Rasadnik" and that at the bottom of the page he gave the name, the initials being "MU." Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 26044, as marked by the witness, receives number P6831, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say in paragraph 31 of your statement, D691, that you went to Rasadnik on a number of occasions. And I'm done with this image. You testified in the Karadzic case that you only dropped by on three occasions and spent half an hour there because your relative, Mirko Vujic, was one of the Serbs in military detention there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a couple of times or three times, yes, I think so. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say in paragraph 31 again, that: "I went to Rasadnik to observe its operation and no guard or detainee ever mentioned to me any inhumane or brutal treatment or claimed that some people were being mistreated," and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down while reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My question is: Is it correct that your observation of the functioning of the Rasadnik facility consisted of dropping by on three occasions for half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You also say that some of the guards there were from the civilian police and some were from the military police. Beginning in late 1992, the camp commander was Vinko Bojic; right?
