utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he was in the Rogatica Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you say that persons were exchanged from Rasadnik and that you have no personal involvement in those exchanges. Your brigade was involved in those exchanges, however; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the brigade did, because it was within its remit to conduct exchanges at the military level. But if it went through the ICRC rather than the brigade, then the ICRC was in charge of such exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, finally, I want to ask you about one specific incident regarding Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could 65 ter 31327.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this, as it comes up, is the judgement against Drago Paunovic in the Bosnian state court. He was convicted of taking a group of Muslim civilians out of Rasadnik camp, ordering their execution, and directly participating in that execution, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. He was not one who took them out because he was away from Rasadnik, maybe 15 to 20 kilometres away. It was done by another person. That person brought them in that particular area and then it happened, what happened. And then Paunovic did what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think perhaps my question was unclear. I hadn't meant physically taking them out. The person that physically transported them, in fact, and has been convicted of doing so in the Bosnian state court was Radisav Ljubinac; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Radisav Ljubinac? Ljubinac, Radisav.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think the transcript might be slightly unclear so I'm going to ask that again. Radisav Ljubinac, in the Bosnian court, was convicted, among other things, of taking these people out of Rasadnik to Duljevac, right, where they he were eventually executed?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Radisav Ljubinac took the people by truck to Paunovic Pero's company, and they met their end there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified as a defence witness in the Paunovic trial; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you're aware now that one of the people taken out who survived was at the time a 15-year-old boy named Armin Bazdar; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. Armin Bazdar. Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Taking you back now to August 1992, you heard about this crime on the same day or the following day; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said so a few days ago. I think I heard it either in the evening that same day or the next day. In any case, I heard about it quite soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified in the Karadzic case that you learned about this through overhearing a conversation between the local Kozici unit commander and someone else; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So it was the same day in the evening or the next day. So that is the only possible difference. By that time, it was known what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you've confirmed that the Kozici unit commander was, in fact, Mr. Paunovic. Who he was talking to?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't remember. I don't know whether he talked to someone or one of his subordinates who mentioned that information. I don't think he was involved in saying that. I think it must have been one of his subordinate commanders who told it to someone, but I don't know who exactly. And that's how I learned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, you heard over --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I'm looking at the clock and I'm also looking at your time sheet at this moment. How much time would you still think you'd need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I would say about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then you will have five minutes and then we'll take the break, and that's, then, the end of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So the Kozici unit commander who was making this call, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he said that our side sustained great losses in the Jacen area. It was a stronghold, an elevation facing the Serb village of Borac, which had been razed to the ground and civilians killed. In an attempt to pass by the village of Borac, they encountered strong fire. And then those people were needed as a human shield, as it was said at that time, and then we know what became of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What did he say about what became of it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, he reported that he suffered manpower losses and that he himself was wounded and that he wanted a human shield --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question -- you have explained that already. What did you -- what did he say about what became of it? Because you were rather vague. Mr. Traldi wants to know what he said what happened then, after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean after the people were brought in that sector? I'm unclear as to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me be very specific, sir, because I have limited time. What did this commander say specifically about the execution of these people that informed you the crime had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He just said that the group had been killed. Without specifying how many, he just said that the group had been killed. At the time, and now, it struck me as unthinkable or unbelievable. It was no one's orders; it was his own initiative. It was his order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "it was his order," you're referring to Mr. Paunovic, one of the battalion commanders in the brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you learnt this, did you keep that information to yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. From the position I was at that moment, I sent that information to my superior, the secretary of the secretariat in Pale in writing. I don't know what he did to relay it to his superior. I don't have that information, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that was Mitar Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you testified in the Paunovic case that he told you that the army had done this; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You also told the chief of police about the massacre?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because our offices were in the same building but on different floors. I simply drew his attention to this in a conversation, and he said, But it was done by the army, and I said, Yes, well, the people involved were civilians --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last sentence of his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat what you said after the word "civilians."

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, Yes, if it was done by the army, then civilians were hurt, and I am just telling you as the police commander that some civilians were killed. I don't know what he did after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Did you inform your commander, Mr. Kusic?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He knew the same day I did. Perhaps we learned about it the same day, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you and he inform your superior command in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose the commander mentioned it in his combat report, which he drafted daily. I think he did. And if he did not, it was a fatal mistake to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the Karadzic case that only after some investigation a few days later, you found out that Mr. Paunovic was the perpetrator. In fact, you knew the same day that it was him who had done this; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it was him the same day. There was some speculation or doubt that he could be the executor. Later on, as it turned out, after an investigation, it was established that it was he who had done it and that the initial information was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You also did not tell the court in his case that you knew he was the perpetrator, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I just answered the questions by the defence and the court. If I was asked that, I answered. And if a particular question was not put to me, there was no answer that I needed to provide. Had I been asked, I would have answered the same way I'm answering you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So rather than punishing your subordinate who had committed mass murder, you testified on his behalf when he was finally put on trial more than a decade later and did not inform the court that he was guilty; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't asked about it. I couldn't have punished him or anyone else without a judgement. So, as far as I was concerned, he wasn't punished because I had my superior who was best placed or in charge of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And your superior didn't punish him either, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he spent a long time in treatment because he himself was wounded. However, what happened later on, I don't know because I never went back to the area. I know that shortly afterwards he left Kozici and Rogatica municipality and went to an unknown location. As far as we were concerned, unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. We'll take a break. Could the witness already be escorted out of the courtroom. How much time would you need after the break, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think a bit more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite a bit, but let's see how it develops. The last portion of the evidence, Mr. Traldi, when evaluating or assessing that evidence, it may be important for the Chamber to know what the witness stated in view of a duty of a witness to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The witness told us that he was not asked about whether Mr. Paunovic was guilty or not. Now, even if such a direct question was not put to him, it may well be that he was asked questions which would require him, if telling the whole truth, to bore the subject himself. Therefore, it would be interesting, perhaps, for the Chamber to know in order to be able to assess the credibility and reliability of the witness's evidence, to know a bit more about what he was asked about. Is there any documentary evidence which would shed some light on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've uploaded the transcript as 65 ter 31449. The transcript is only in B/C/S. We have acquired audio in both B/C/S and English, and we're happy to provide whatever would assist the Chamber in evaluating the evidence, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we could ask him a few questions about how far away the questions that were put to him were from the question about guilt or innocence. And I do understand that we don't have the English materials to further explore in this context. We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ujic, before I give an opportunity to the Defence to re-examine you, I have one or a few questions about your testimony in the case against Mr. Paunovic. You said you didn't tell the court that you knew that he was the perpetrator because you were not asked about it. What were the questions about when you appeared as a witness in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't remember the questions, but I know that in my written statement I described my activities when I was president of the executive committee. That means before the war and the early days of war. Later on, as I stated, this incident happened, and I was asked, although I don't know what the questions were, about my knowledge relating to that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you asked about your knowledge about, as you call it, the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, yes. And I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you did not -- and then did you not tell them that a few days after the incident you learned that Mr. Paunovic was the perpetrator or the most likely perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I wasn't asked directly, I didn't provide indirect answers. If not, then I couldn't give any direct answers, because if they wanted to ask me that, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two ways of asking that question. The one is: Do you know anything about the perpetrators? Was a question of that kind asked to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, as much as I would like to remember, I really cannot recall the question. I gave the answers as I did. You can probably have my testimony, so can you see what the questions were put and the answers that I gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Or would you consider only the question "Was Mr. Paunovic the perpetrator" a question upon which you would have had to answer that, to your knowledge, he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I believe. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is that, then, the whole truth, or is that -- as a witness, you're obliged to answer questions in accordance with the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. If someone asks you without even mentioning Mr. Paunovic about possible perpetrators, wouldn't you consider it to be the whole truth to tell that court, if such a question was asked, also about what you meanwhile knew about him possibly being a perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused about you telling us, on the one hand side, that you don't remember the questions, and at the same time telling us that you were not asked the question which would have triggered you to answer that Mr. Paunovic was, to your knowledge, the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, if a judge asks me a question requesting a direct answer, I was therefore not given any time to expand on it. I was expected to give a direct answer. Whatever the chamber asked me, I provided them straightforward answers without expanding it further on because they want me to specifically answer this or that, and that what's I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I take it that they also wanted to hear from you the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, an assumption is one thing. However, whether the questions were put in that way is another assumption. But, as I said, I provided answers to the best of my ability and with the intention of telling the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The wish of the Chamber to learn more about the questioning of the witness remains. I'm looking at the parties, whether a selection could be made or after translations are there. But it is a relevant issue in relation to the reliability and the credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Paunovic judgement available?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it available in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, in both languages. I called it up towards the end of the examination and I neglected to tender it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But I do so now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do so now. Madam Registrar, could you please give a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I reminded of the 65 ter number. Is it 31327?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Ms. Stewart, as usual, is the ultimate authority and confirms that our recollections are correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31327 receives number P6832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Could we have that document on our screen, page 11, please, in English, and I don't know whether we have the B/C/S version there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The P number is not recorded. Perhaps it could be repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31327 receives number P6832.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is admitted into evidence. And could we have a look at page 11. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I read from that judgement and it's at the bottom of the page. And I most likely will have not the correct B/C/S page, but I read to you one line of that sentence: "Only witness Mile Ujic said that he had heard about the crime on the same day or the following day and added that it had been committed by some extremists." Apparently, that is what that court recorded as your testimony, that you had told them that it had been committed by some extremists; whereas you tell us that you knew within a couple of days that it was Mr. Paunovic who was the likely perpetrator. Now, you told us that you had not been asked about it, but apparently questions about the incident itself were put to you. Otherwise, I would not expect to have this record of your statement. Have you any comment on your testimony in that case, that you thought that it had been committed by some extremists rather than by Mr. Paunovic, as you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain. When I said here that I had heard about that on the afternoon of the same day or the perhaps the next day, there were rumours that it had been perpetrated by Mr. Paunovic but it wasn't corroborated that he was exactly the one who did it. When I said that those were extremists, I stand by that, because a normal person couldn't do that but, rather, an extremist who is insane and with disturbed mind. That's why I gave this answer. Of course, I do not rule out him as the executor, and he was convicted in the court of law. In my eyes, this is not a normal behavior. It has to do with a disturbed mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then look at what you told us about rumours or what you knew. I think you told us but let me just -- one second, please. I read one of your answers to you: "I didn't know it was him the same day. There was some speculation or doubt that he could be the executor. Later on, as it turned out, after an investigation, it was established that it was he who had done it and that the initial information was correct." This is not rumour but this is the finding on the basis of an investigation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you allow me, at first there were some suspicions as to whether he was the a perpetrator. Some thought he was; some thought that nobody knew. However, after the investigation, it was confirmed that he was, indeed, the culprit. And I think I mentioned that this morning in my responses to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Investigation by whom and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether it was conducted by security organs from the brigade immediately in those days, and I think it was them, and that they obtained this information through their own channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you testified ten years after that they were some extremists, you were not telling the truth, were you? Because you knew through this investigation that it had been established that it was Mr. Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I was speaking about the first pieces of information that I received, that it had been done either by him or with other persons. This was the initial information. Later on, corroborated information was provided that he was the sole perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So ten years after that, before a court in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you knew exactly what was established by that investigation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, of course, I learned about that, both through the indictment and through the questions put to me by the defence team and by reviewing some of the materials. Therefore, I was familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us a second ago that it was through the investigation of the brigade that you learned about this. That's not the indictment ten years later. That is pretty shortly after the event you learned about it. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, but that was later that I learned that he was the executor -- executioner. But I wasn't asked specifically about that in the court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but you added apparently to the questions that these were extremists where you knew well that the investigations of the brigade had revealed that it was Mr. Paunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first information that I had was that it had been done by a group of extremists. Only later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but ten years after that, as you told us, you knew it and you didn't tell that court in Bosnia-Herzegovina what you knew, and that this -- but please tell me when I'm wrong, but that you were not telling the whole of the truth. Because, by then, you knew that investigations had revealed that Paunovic was the perpetrator, not a group of extremists. And I leave it alone, whether you consider Mr. Paunovic to be an extremist, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I reiterate, I answered only the questions that were put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Those questions were about who perpetrated this crime apparently. At least I have difficulties in understanding it in any other way. I think I have given you ample opportunity to explain yourself. Let's move on. Mr. Lukic, if you're ready to re-examine the witness, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon once again, Mr. Ujic.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will dwell only briefly on what has just been discussed. After this incident, how much time elapsed before you continued your job at the Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that a few days later I left the brigade forever, and I continued to work as the chief in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any official report on the investigation carried out by the brigade in the aftermath of the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received anything official or in writing. Everything was conveyed orally, and that is why perhaps the answers were as they were because the brigade had never provided me with a written report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on, when you were the secretary of the National Defence, did you receive any reports from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, I never received anything from the brigade, neither combat reports, except their requests for additional mobilisation or mobilisation for work obligation. That's the only thing that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now call P6823. It's a document dated 25th of March, 1992, a document produced by the -- or received, rather, by the SDS from Sveto Veselinovic, Tomo Batinic, and yourself, in which you informed them about your resignation. You can see in the second paragraph of this statement it reads that: "The factual division on the ground is already in existence but that the official division must be accompanied by laws issued by relevant Serbian ministries, as well as party agreements on the highest level." So do you know whether there was any agreement reached between the SDS and the SDA at the highest level with regard to the division of Rogatica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were negotiations going between the Muslim and the Serb negotiators to divide the municipality, the police administration, even the buildings, and the undisputed part of the territory where either of the peoples were in majority. That was also included.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, we don't have much time. Can you tell me whether the leadership of the SDA and the SDS ever discussed this division because obviously you were waiting for such an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what should have happened; at least that's what we were informed about in Rogatica. However, that never happened because the first killings took place on the 6th of May, and all the negotiations and agreements were put on hold because the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Rajko Kusic, was he above you in the SDS structure? What was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was above me because he was a member of the Main Board of the Serbian Democratic Party and, as such, he operated in Rogatica as SDS number one. He would be the one to convey instructions from the Main Board. He would issue orders in meetings about the next actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified about Sokolovic. What did you mean when you said that a group of people told you that he was tougher than you? What were you exactly told? You were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says in my statement that he was tougher than myself. I understood that to mean that I lacked political experience, that he was an old timer in the politics because he was two times in the office of the president of the municipality, and since he was in party for such a long time, he had experience, unlike me, who came from the industrial sector, and what followed was this infamous dismissal of mine and his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly look at P6773.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: With regard to this document, it was suggested to you that the Serbian side abandoned the negotiations on division. I'd like to focus your attention on paragraph 3. You can see it on the screen in front of you. It says that an agreement was reached to divide the territory of Rogatica into two parts, the Muslim and the Serbian one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you were on your feet. You are not anymore, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we had the appropriate part of the English, which we hadn't yet and I believe it's been solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "The Serbian Assembly of Rogatica municipality based on its decisions of the 18th of May, 1992, rendered null and void as a result of the outbreak of war, triggered by the killing of Serbian soldier by members of the Green Berets who was killed from an ambush exactly in the territory that under the agreement reached should have been allocated to the Serbian municipality of Rogatica." Do you know who was killed before the 18th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Bakacovic [phoen] was killed on the 6th of May who was a civilian. Members of the Ristic family were killed at that Madjar, near Rogatica around the 11th or 15th of May. That was the reason, actually, the war broke out, and the agreed division no longer took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it in the territory that was supposed to be controlled by the Serbs or by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all happened at the same time as the division was being agreed and in the territory that belonged to the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, was it demanded that the body of a soldier be returned? Did you take part in that -- in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was on the negotiating team of the Serbian people from day one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What were you told when you demanded that body?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a very defeating answer because it was contrary to what had previously been agreed on. Then they said when we kill the next dozen or 100 Serbs, only then will we give back all the bodies. So there was -- that was way too much, and the decision was made to renege on the agreement on our side because the war was already underway and people were being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- because Muslims often changed members of their negotiating team because some were milder or more skilful whereas others were not. But on that day, it was Ramiz Alajbegovic, as the police station commander, and a judge of the Rogatica basic court, Adnan Suljagic. They said it at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's rather repetitious what you were asking, that what was said is clear from the statement. Who said it? Ramiz Alajbegovic also appears in the statement. So why do we need to hear that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were the Chief of Staff of the brigade. Did you ever act on behalf of the commander? Did you ever stand in for him?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about two people. It is in the temporary transcript of this case, page 17, line 24.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Page 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apparently two members of the Rogatica Brigade were disciplined for killing a non-Serb, and that they received one-month prison sentence. Were they sanctioned to that term or were they simply held in custody in detention that lasted for a month, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the court issued its judgement and they were held in custody in Rogatica and later they were sent to the detention of the Vlasenica prison, to the detention unit of that prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, page 70 of what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of the -- transcript from the 16th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it has meanwhile been -- we will find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now page 26.930.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I couldn't open this transcript on the web mail so I couldn't check the new pages, but thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to ask you is this: Was the sentence they received a month or longer?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a month in Rogatica, they were held in the remand prison. The sentence was longer, and when it was pronounced they were sent to the Drina Corps facility, that is to say, the jail in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have P6827 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the date of this document. It is the 22nd of May, 1992. The SRK command on that day sent an order to the Rogatica Brigade command, the brigade of the TO, that is. I don't know if you can recall it today, but on the 22nd of May, 1992, was the Rogatica Brigade part of the VRS? Were the two organisations functioning in parallel, or was it still the case that this TO body of the Rogatica municipality was integrated into the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO existed until the first day the VRS came into being. When it came into existence, that part of the Rogatica TO was incorporated into the VRS. This date seems odd. There was a previous incorporation with the Army of Republika Srpska, and now we have the 22nd of May, 1992 by which time the TO no longer existed. It was the armed forces. Because there could not have been that there were TO and the army functioning at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The next page, please, under (j) in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 22nd of May, we see that "The Rogatica TO brigade shall be formed from or in the territory of Rogatica," so in the future tense. The brigade commander was to be Bogdan Kusic.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It couldn't have been Bogdan Kusic. There was no Bogdan Kusic. It could only have been Rajko Kusic. So this is a typographical error. It is true that the Rogatica Brigade, as part of the TO, functioned as such until the VRS was established. When the armed forces were established or perhaps a few days later, it was incorporated. It is believed in our part of the country that as of the 20th of May, all members of the Rogatica TO became members of the VRS, and that is what their files reflect in the office of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is this order about, then, when it orders that the Rogatica Brigade of the TO be established on the 22nd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you don't, you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P166, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the 23rd of May, 1992. You have explained why it says "Ljubljana" on the stamp when asked by Judge Orie. However, I'm interested in why these attacks began. The document states in the fifth line in the B/C/S, which is line 5 in the English as well, it says: "The body of a soldier who had been captured by enemy forces two days ago has been recovered." Is it the body of the soldier you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the direct cause of that fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting was caused directly by the inability to recover the late man's body, to have it buried. His friends -- his family lived perhaps 300 metres away from the place he was killed, and the other side refused. They said, When we kill a dozen, then we'll give the bodies back. And then the commander decided to resort to force to retrieve the body, and it was, indeed, done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at P6828 next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I did understand that retrieving the body that the other side was refusing to return to you was in a small area, whereas what is described here seems to be a rather large and broad operation against several villages and settlements. Was that all aimed at retrieving that body of that killed person, or was it a more general attack to get control over a larger area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct. All those villages were majority Muslim villages, and the concentration of Muslim forces was quite high in that area. We were attacked by mortars from those villages. Our positions, therefore, had to respond, attacking those villages so as to secure access to that area. That is why those villages were attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we have P4387 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The date is the 23rd of June, 1992. You were asked about it when questions were being put to you about Mr. Mehmed Agic.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph, it reads: "A group of enemy extremists headed by Mehmed Agic, one of the founders of the TO in which he worked for many years, was captured in the sector of Vragolovi."

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It goes on: "Weapons and smaller quantities of devices with dynamite were found in their possession." Did you know at that time that Mr. Agic was actually captured as an enemy soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We dealt with it here already. I said that I was informed by radio communication that he had been arrested, and I came to the Sladara factory immediately upon his arrival. I believe I was the first person to visit him. I know he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Agic survive the war?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Nowadays he works in a federal ministry as an expert of some sort, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's briefly look at P6828.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Mr. Lukic, I wasn't sure whether you were done with Mr. Agic. Do you know of any reason why Mr. Agic would tell things that you consider to be totally untrue in respect of yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I responsibly claim, being aware of his statement I was shown here, I said so about Mr. Agic, I said that we were neighbours living in the same apartment block. I said that he was in charge of the TO, the former Rogatica municipality, the joint one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told all that. But is there any specific reason you could think of why Mr. Agic would not -- in accordance with the truth as you tell us, would have told about your behaviour when you were visiting him, that is, such as beating up and -- why would he tell that? Do you know any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, my only explanation is that he would portray himself as a victim and that he was tortured as officer. Now, for me, kicking him, which is not something that a sane person would say, that's not true. I simply gave him a cigarette. I lit it up for him. He was tied up, but he didn't appear frightened at the time and for the few minutes he spoke to me. I left the room, and he stayed behind with Mr. Kusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "tied up"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was tied at the time he was arrested and transported to the malt factory. I don't know whether he exactly had handcuffs on, but he was bound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And he was blindfolded, lying on the floor; is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. He recognised my voice, though, when I entered. He said, Hi neighbour, do you have a cigarette? And I gave him one. We spoke for less than five minutes. Commander Kusic came and Kusic said, So what are you doing? You came to see your neighbour? And I said, Yes. But then he said, You have no business here, leave. And I did. Whether something happened later is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you consider it a normal conversation, even if someone is detained lying on the floor, blindfolded, only being able to recognise you through your voice? Is that -- did you give any comment on that to Mr. Kusic or did you do anything about that type of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Mr. Kusic said while I was present since Mr. Agic was the commander of the joint TO Staff where Kusic was the soldier, he told him then, Boss - that's what they referred to like to Agic - yesterday you commanded me and now I have you tied up. So a private arrested a captain first class. That's what I heard, and then I left. I don't know what followed. I also heard him say this: You are an officer, and we respect your rank. You will be treated accordingly, meaning you will not be tortured, beaten, but you are going to write a statement about your organisation, your weapons, who planted antitank mines in the town, and so on and so forth. And Agic said, I will write down everything I know. Indeed, he signed that statement, although I never saw it because it was handed directly to the commander. I don't know what's in it. I do know he provided a written statement, though. As for his statement to the court where he says I kicked him, it is untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can have P6828, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ujic, we can see the document from the Rogatica Brigade dated 31st May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of the page, it reads, under the heading: "Request," the penultimate sentence says: "We have many unarmed men." What was the situation like towards the end of May on the ground? Were there any unarmed men? What kind of problems did the Serbian side encounter?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This request portrayed the exact situation on the ground. We were poorly armed during that period, and as he said, he is asking for 25 automatic rifles and five machine-guns. This is something for a brigade. However, in terms of villages, it is just a token quantity. However, they wanted to be stronger and to reinforce their capacity because, at that time, they were pretty weak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 16 of today's transcript, line -- lines 12 through 14, there's mention of Kozadre and the fighting that took place there in which you took part. The Prosecutor asked you about it, and I'm going to read both your -- both the question and your answer in English and you will receive a proper interpretation. [In English] I quote: "It would be a legitimate military" -- sorry: "Q. Your view at that time was if there's fire coming from a village, it's not a village anymore. It's a military target; right? "A. It would be a legitimate military target, yes." [Interpretation] What I'd like to ask you is whether you opened fire on the entire village or only the targets that you spotted.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I responsibly claim that we didn't fire randomly but only engaged the targets or the locations that we discovered enemy fire coming from. So this was not discriminate firing and this was not indiscriminate fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This clears, Your Honour, what you wanted to clarify, does it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly. Discriminate or indiscriminate. Although I have one additional question for the witness. Fire that came from those villages, what type of fire was it? Was it machine-gun fire? Was it automatic rifles? Was it mortars? What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were submachine-guns and 60-millimetre mortars. Of course, there were automatic weapon, rifles, and the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you able to see or was there any civilian column at all trying to pull out of the area?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can claim with full responsibility that, in spite of my best effort to spot this column, which, as a rule, took their route along the ravines and streambeds and valleys which were not accessible. However, fire was opened at us from higher ground and from the locations that we eventually managed to reveal. I have to say that that was not volley of shells. It was a limited number of shells and we used them only to engage very specific targets with the best possible accuracy, and I was the one who provided grid reference points for these targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have P4387. [In English] Sorry, I finished with this one. I need P6803. And this would be my last document and last line of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you mean 6830?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 6803. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 6803 Mr. Lukic asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript says something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have it on our screens. It's the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was mention of some large-scale activities. It says: "No significant enemy activity in the brigade's zone of responsibility were observed." Do you know what was meant by "significant activities"?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, significant activities meant large-scale attacks on either Serb villages or separation, line but on that day when the report is sent nothing of that sort happened. What we see further on, we see that people were afraid of the war and they were seeking to be taken to a safe place to avoid war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may talk to my client for half a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the volume please be lowered. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ujic, do you know the strength of the Muslim forces in Rogatica that was under their control?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a brigade, and I must say they were well armed, well trained and well skilled, especially for sabotage and terrorist actions, for the raids of sabotage groups who would penetrate the rear of the territory, commit what they intend to do, and then quickly retreat. And they were very good at it, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ujic, did history play any role in the attitude of the people in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, definitely yes. 1941 was not a long time ago, and it will not quickly be forgotten, when two Muslim soldiers or, rather, two Ustasha would take 100 civilians, women, old people, children, and then slaughter them and they burned them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness has answered your question by saying, "Unfortunately, definitely yes," and I think it's clear from a lot of evidence that the history and the way in which the various ethnicities and groups treated each other during the Second World War and even before that, and after that, was certainly part of feelings among the population. If that was your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was my last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I do need about five minutes and I'm in the Chamber's hands as to whether to do it before or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31409.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As this comes to the screen, sir, at temporary transcript page 61 today, Mr. Lukic ask you: "Q. I will dwell only briefly on what has just been discussed. After this incident, how much time elapsed before you continued your job at the Secretariat for National Defence?" Now, you understood that Mr. Lukic, like you, was using this incident to describe Mr. Paunovic's crime, the mass murder of people taken from Rasadnik; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You answered: "It is possible that a few days later I left the brigade forever, and I continued to work as the chief in Rogatica." Now, what we're seeing on the screen is an order dated 15 December 1992 from your commander, Rajko Kusic, sent to the Drina Corps command. It is appointing officers to positions in the command of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. Now, just to confirm, by 15 December 1992, the Rogatica Brigade had been renamed the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade and had been transferred to the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you read what we find at point 1, please, on this page. Could you read it off the document aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Brigade staff: Item 1, as chief of brigade staff: Mile (father's name Dobroslav) Ujic, captain first class. Personal military occupational speciality, 31202. Personal identification number, 2505951173233." So these are my personal details. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, I have a question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is four months after the massacre of the people taken from Rasadnik to be used as human shields, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's not possible that you left the brigade just a few days after that massacre, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be happy to give you an answer. The minister of Defence, General Bogdan Subotic, issued a decision appointing me officially as the secretary of the Secretariat of Defence in late June or early July 1992. However, I remained a member of the staff of the brigade as an acting chief of the brigade staff. That is why these two offices overlapped because I was in the brigade and in the draft office at the same time. And since he did not have a person with proper speciality for this, my name remained there virtually as working both in the brigade and in the draft office as of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you continued working in the brigade during this period, December 1992, as your commander, Mr. Kusic, is informing the Drina Corps command; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to say that most of my time I spent at the defence office, and I went to the brigade as needed every day or every other day for a couple of hours in order to instruct the soldiers in artillery skills and other skills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to be perfectly clearly, what I'm putting to you is when you told Mr. Lukic that it was possible that you left the brigade command, that you left the brigade forever, a few days after Mr. Paunovic killed those people, that wasn't the truth. You didn't leave the brigade forever at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being a chief is one thing and being an acting chief is a totally different thing, pending the replacement. I informed -- or, actually, I was appointed by the minister in late June or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You've been asked to repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it is true that I received the decision from the minister of defence appointing me the chief of the office in Rogatica. Whenever my presence in the brigade was necessary for an hour or two, I would go there, finish my job, and return again to the draft office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 31353. I believe it's been assigned an exhibit number. I'm looking for page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P6824, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't have the B/C/S page off the top of my head, but if we could just look in the middle here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is the statement you gave the Rogatica police in 2004. Middle of the second paragraph, you said: "I had been in charge of one of the companies called Gucevska until sometime in early May 1992 when the brigade command reassigned me to the position of the brigade chief. I held this position throughout the entire 1992." Again, what you told the Rogatica police, 2004, that was the truth. You were the brigade chief through the entire 1992 and afterwards; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is only one truth, which is what I said, that originally I was in charge of the TO Gucevo; that the brigade command summoned me sometime in May, asking me to hand over the company command to somebody else and that I would be transferred to the brigade. However, already in July, I was appointed chief of the defence department. I only went to the brigade from time to time as an acting Chief of Staff because soon thereafter, my replacement was found. A new officer came to take my place, and I definitely stopped going to the brigade except when it was necessary to work with the soldiers and train them on how to detect targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I put to you that you're modifying your evidence today and you're doing so to minimise your own responsibility. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE UJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I am not trying to diminish responsibility. I was what I was. It can be documented. Whatever I did, I am here. If I did something wrong, I am at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 31409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31409 receives number P6833, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just very briefly. I am aware we have a document bearing the witness's name after this date in our collection. I'm in the Chamber's hands. I hadn't uploaded it previously and I don't have the ERN in my notes, but if the Chamber would wish him to be given an opportunity to comment, we can locate it during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the statement from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: A document from the brigade bearing his name, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And dated?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: After the 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the 15th of December. We'll consider it, whether we need it or not but -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement of Mr. Agic you referred to, is that in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are not tendering it. You read the relevant portions and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic, any further questions? No. Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Ujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I think -- no, I think we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes your evidence, Mr. Ujic. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It all took more time than expected and therefore the Chamber is a bit sorry for the next witness who may have been waiting, but it really doesn't make any sense to start for five minutes with him and then immediately -- so, therefore, I would suggest that we adjourn for the day and that we start with the next witness tomorrow. And could VWS tell the witness that the Chamber is sorry that we kept him waiting for such a long time and could not start his testimony today. We'll adjourn and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 21st of October, Courtroom I, 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 21st day of October, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.51 p.m.,
